Period schedule:

Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Entering the Story: Unlikely Friendships and First Read

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.39): pre-reading activation — friendship sentences, share with class.
Let us read (p.39): discuss meaning of 'unlikely'; think of unlikely friends.

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading prompt from 'Let us read' (p.39): invite students to think about what friends mean to them and complete the 'With my friend I…' sentences. A few volunteers share their completed sentences aloud.

Turn to the title 'The Unlikely Best Friends' and ask groups to discuss the word 'unlikely' (p.39) — what might it mean here? Invite examples of unlikely friends from students' own lives or from films and stories they know.

Conduct an unhurried shared read-aloud of the narrative (pp.39–44, Part I), with students following in their textbooks. Pause at natural breaks — the dog entering the stable, the bathing scene — to let the story settle before continuing.

Close with a brief whole-class moment: ask students to hold one image from the story in mind — the elephant spraying the dog or the dog sleeping in the stable — as a prompt for the discussion that will follow when they return to the text.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading sentences (p.39) warm up personal experience before the text's animal friendship is introduced; let several different voices be heard, including quieter students. 'Unlikely' is a key term the whole story hangs on — resist giving the definition immediately; group guessing sharpens prediction skills. Tasks covering the mid-story pause questions (p.42) and remaining comprehension passages are available as self-study in the 'Let us discuss' and 'Let us think and reflect' sections.
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for recording student suggestions about 'unlikely'

periods.activity_title: Deep Reading: Grief, Generosity, and What Friendship Means

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.45): why Gajaraj refused food; who friends are at story's end.
Let us think and reflect (p.45–46): analogy — mahout : kind :: Gajaraj : ___; friend vs caretaker.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.45): two examples showing Gajaraj's happiness with a friend.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud Part II of the narrative (pp.44–45) — the separation, the grief of both animals, the farmer's decision, and Buntee's joyful return — with students following in their textbooks.

Whole-class discussion of the 'Let us discuss' questions (p.45): why Gajaraj stopped eating, and who forms new friendships by the story's end. Encourage students to support answers with specific moments from the narrative.

Work through the first extract from 'Let us think and reflect' (pp.45–46): the analogy question (mahout : kind :: Gajaraj : ___) and the open question distinguishing a friend from a caretaker. Pairs discuss the distinction before sharing with the class.

Invite one or two students to offer a single sentence capturing what makes Gajaraj's relationship with Buntee different from his relationship with the mahout, drawing the discussion to a close on the story's central idea.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full narrative, students are now positioned to feel the weight of the separation episode — let the emotional texture surface in discussion before moving to analytical questions. The friend-versus-caretaker distinction (p.46) is the conceptual heart of this unit; give it time and resist closing the question too quickly. The second extract passage (p.46, farmer and rope questions) and the reflective questions on Buntee licking the farmer's hand and what was 'unlikely' about the friendship are available as self-study in 'Let us think and reflect'.
materials: Blackboard for noting student responses to the analogy question

periods.activity_title: A Cow and a Leopard: Listening for Detail and Sequence

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.49): fill missing details in paragraph using exact story words.
Let us listen (p.50): number sentences in correct sequence after second listening.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening activity: tell students they will hear a true account of another unlikely friendship — a cow and a leopard from Vadodara, Gujarat. Ask them to keep their books closed and simply listen on the first reading.
Read the transcript aloud at a measured pace (p.71 of the textbook). Students then open to the fill-in paragraph (p.49) and complete the missing details using exact words from what they heard.

Discuss the completed paragraph briefly: invite two or three students to read their answers aloud. Clarify any words students found difficult to catch — 'domestic', 'regularly', 'attacked' — before the second listening.

Read the transcript a second time. Students then work on the sequencing task (p.50) — numbering the four sentences in the order events occurred. Pairs compare and agree on their final sequence before a whole-class check.

Close with a brief oral round: what surprised students most about the cow-and-leopard friendship? Draw a one-sentence parallel to Gajaraj and Buntee's story to anchor the listening content in the chapter's central theme.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript (p.71) is read aloud by the teacher; students do not read it themselves before attempting the tasks. Two readings are built into the plan — the first for global meaning, the second for the precise sequence — so students experience the difference between listening for gist and listening for order. The word 'domestic' may be unfamiliar; a brief gloss during the mid-activity pause is enough without over-explaining before the listening.
materials: Blackboard to write the four sequence sentences for the class check

periods.activity_title: Same, Different, Both: Talking About a Real Friend

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.47): interview a partner; share similarities and differences with class.

time_bands.activity: Remind students of the Gajaraj-and-Buntee friendship: two creatures with nothing obviously in common who still found joy in each other. Ask: what do you actually share with your closest friend, and what is completely different? This question launches the speaking task.

Students work in pairs using the cue frame from 'Let us speak' (p.47) — filling in likes, dislikes and shared interests for themselves and their partner. Each student takes a turn interviewing the other, making brief notes as they listen.

Each pair stands and shares: one student speaks two or three sentences about their friend using the sentence starters provided ('My friend and I like…'; 'I like … but my friend likes…'; 'We are different as…'). The teacher models register and encourages full sentences.

After several pairs have shared, the class identifies the words that keep coming up to express similarity and difference — 'both', 'but', 'unlike', 'neither'. Write these on the board as a shared vocabulary resource drawn directly from students' own speech.
Close by asking one student to sum up in a single sentence what the class discovered: can two very different people still be best friends? Link the answer back to the story's central idea.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who are shy about speaking in front of the class often manage the pair interview more comfortably than the full-class share; build confidence in the pair stage before calling on volunteers for the whole-class round. The cue words listed in the speaking task ('same', 'different', 'but', 'both', 'unlike') bridge naturally into the writing task; surfacing them on the board here gives students a resource they can draw on independently.
materials: Blackboard for collecting similarity/difference vocabulary from student responses

periods.activity_title: Six Sentences About My Friend: Drafting, Responding, Revising

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.47): six sentences about a friend — similarities, differences, linking words.

time_bands.activity: Display on the board the linking word list from 'Let us write' (p.47): same, different, and, but, both, still, like, unlike, neither, nor, either, or. Briefly show students what one sentence looks like using each type — a similarity sentence, a difference sentence, and a contrast sentence.

Students write their six sentences independently, drawing on the facts they gathered about their friend in the speaking activity and using the linking words as guides. The teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with the question 'What is one thing only your friend does, not you?'

Paired peer response: students exchange their writing with a partner and read each other's sentences. Each reader underlines one linking word used well and puts a question mark next to any sentence that is not clear. Writers then read the question-marked sentence aloud to themselves and decide whether to revise it.

Students revise and finalise their six sentences in their notebooks. Two or three volunteers read their completed writing to the class; the class listens for which linking words they used and whether the piece captures both similarity and difference.

Close with a brief teacher comment on what made the shared pieces effective — specific detail, varied linking words, a balance of similarity and difference — so students leave with concrete criteria they applied in this sitting.

periods.teacher_notes: The linking-word list (p.47) is the structural scaffold for this task; displaying it throughout the writing time prevents students from defaulting to 'and' and 'but' exclusively. Peer response is kept tightly focused — one positive marking and one question mark — so it remains quick and useful rather than becoming a rewriting exercise. Students who finish early may add a seventh sentence expressing how the friendship makes them feel, using language from the story.

periods.activity_title: Opposites, Past Tenses, and Neither/Either: Language in the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.47): crossword puzzle — opposites of clue words from the story.
Let us learn (p.48): sort story verbs into Simple Past, Past Progressive, Past Perfect columns.
Let us learn (p.49): discuss and practise neither/nor and either/or with example sentences.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.49): choose correct past-tense verb form to complete the farmer-and-Buntee passage.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the opposites crossword (p.47): all clue words come from the story students have read. Work the first two clues together as a class — 'unkind' and 'yelped' — so students see that word meaning is drawn from narrative context, not abstract definition. Students then complete the remaining clues in pairs.

Turn to the verb-sorting table (p.48): display the three column headings — Simple Past, Past Progressive, Past Perfect — on the board with one example in each. Students read the list of story verbs and sort them into the correct column, working individually first, then comparing with a neighbour.

Use the sentence from the story — 'neither the farmer nor the mahout noticed that the two friends were in tears' — as the entry point for discussing 'neither/nor' and 'either/or' (p.49). Work through the two example sentences together, then invite students to make their own sentences about the story or their own lives.

Brief consolidation: ask students to say aloud one new opposite pair they learned from the crossword and one verb from the story in the past progressive. Set the passage completion task (p.49) as homework and explain what students should attend to: which tense fits each blank and why.

periods.teacher_notes: All three grammar points are grounded in the story's own language — the crossword clue words, the narrative verbs, and the sentence about the farmer and the mahout — so students experience grammar as a feature of the text they already know rather than as an abstract rule set. The three-column verb sort (p.48) is the most demanding task here; if students struggle to distinguish Past Progressive from Past Perfect, use 'was/were + -ing' versus 'had + past participle' as quick diagnostic checks. The paragraph completion task (p.49) sent for homework consolidates the tense distinctions practised in class.
materials: Blackboard for the three-column tense table and opposite-pair collection

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Story: Jataka Roots and Real-World Animal Friendships

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.50): class discussion on elephants in Indian culture and ecological challenges.
Let us explore (p.51): read and discuss the Tarra-and-Bella news report from the US sanctuary.

time_bands.activity: Open by sharing the origin note from 'Let us explore' (p.50): the story of Gajaraj and Buntee is adapted from the Jataka tale 'The Elephant and the Dog', part of a two-thousand-year tradition of wisdom stories. Ask students: what kind of lesson do they think these ancient stories were meant to teach?

Whole-class discussion on elephants in Indian culture and contemporary ecological challenges (p.50): the teacher seeds the discussion with two prompts — what roles have elephants played in Indian history, festivals, and religion? And what pressures do elephants face today where their habitats meet human settlements? Students respond and build on each other's ideas.

Read the Tarra-and-Bella news report (p.51) together as a class. Students then discuss in pairs: in what ways is this real friendship similar to Gajaraj and Buntee's? What does the detail of Tarra standing outside the building for three weeks tell us about animal friendship? Pairs share their most striking observation with the class.

Close the chapter with a whole-class reflection: the story began with an elephant longing for a friend and ended with two animals, and then two humans, forming unexpected bonds. Ask students to name in one sentence what the chapter, the Jataka tradition, and the Tarra-Bella account all have in common.

periods.teacher_notes: The Jataka context (p.50) situates the narrative in a living storytelling tradition; students who find the first prompt about lesson-types interesting can be invited to read another Jataka story independently. The ecological discussion may surface strong feelings — habitat loss, human-elephant conflict — and is worth giving space; it connects the chapter's theme of mutual care to a real-world ethical question that middle-stage students are developmentally ready to engage with.
materials: Blackboard for collecting student observations from the Tarra-Bella discussion

items.item_stem:
Read the statements below about the story 'The Unlikely Best Friends' and write True or False for each. Give one reason from the story to support your answer for statement 3.
1. Gajaraj felt lonely even though he lived in a royal stable with comfortable surroundings.
2. The mahout immediately chased the stray dog away when he first noticed it in the stable.
3. Both Gajaraj and Buntee refused to eat after they were separated from each other.

options.text: Gajaraj felt lonely even though he lived in a royal stable with comfortable surroundings.
The mahout immediately chased the stray dog away when he first noticed it in the stable.
Both Gajaraj and Buntee refused to eat after they were separated from each other.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — the story states that Gajaraj longed for a friend despite his royal comforts. 2. False — the mahout tolerated the dog's presence and even threw it crumbs, seeing how happy Gajaraj was. 3. True — the story says neither Gajaraj nor Buntee would eat after the separation; students may cite either animal's refusal as textual support.

items.source_lo: Student identifies textual evidence and infers meaning using narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Gajaraj's loneliness, the elephant-dog friendship, separation grief, mahout and farmer bond.
items.item_stem: By the end of the story, the mahout and the farmer embrace, forming their own unexpected bond. What does this second friendship suggest about the story's central idea? Support your answer with one detail from the narrative about how either man behaved when his animal was in distress.

expected_elements: Friendship crosses species and human boundaries alike.
Mahout tolerated and fed the dog, showing care beyond duty.
Farmer removed the rope, putting Buntee's happiness first.
Human bond mirrors animal bond — mutual care defines both.

items.source_context: Cow-and-leopard friendship from Vadodara; leopard's nocturnal visits; villagers' surprise.
items.item_stem:
After listening to the account of the cow and the leopard from Vadodara, choose the correct answer for each question.

1. What kind of animal is the leopard described as in the story?
A. A domestic animal that lives with humans
B. A wild animal that later became friends with a cow
C. A farm animal kept by the villagers
D. A zoo animal that escaped into the village

2. When did the leopard return to visit the cow after leaving the village?
A. During the morning, when the villagers were awake
B. In the afternoon, when the cow was grazing
C. At night, when the village was quiet
D. On festival days only

options.label: A
options.text: A domestic animal that lives with humans

options.label: B
options.text: A wild animal that later became friends with a cow

options.label: C
options.text: A farm animal kept by the villagers

options.label: D
options.text: A zoo animal that escaped into the village

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the cow's role with the leopard's — applies the domestic label to the wrong animal.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Treats the leopard as a village farm animal; misses the wild-animal contrast central to the account.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a detail about a zoo that does not appear in the transcript.

items.item_stem: The four sentences below describe events from the account of the cow and the leopard. They are not in the order in which the events happened. Write the numbers 1 to 4 to show the correct sequence, with 1 for the first event.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Sentence | Correct order |
|---|---|
| The cow took care of the leopard cub like a mother. | |
| The leopard stopped coming to the village regularly. | |
| The leopard returned at night to sit beside the cow. | |
| The leopard left the village after it grew older. | |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1-cow took care of cub, 2-leopard left village, 3-leopard returned at night, 4-leopard stopped coming regularly.

answer_key.left: The cow took care of the leopard cub like a mother.
The leopard left the village after it grew older.
The leopard returned at night to sit beside the cow.
The leopard stopped coming to the village regularly.

items.item_stem:
The sentences below describe moments from the story. Each sentence has a blank. Choose the correct verb form from the brackets and write it in the blank. Then, for sentence 3, write one new sentence of your own using 'neither … nor' to describe any two characters from the story.

1. When the farmer arrived, Gajaraj _____________ (was eating / had already finished / was missing) Buntee terribly.
2. The mahout _____________ (noticed / was noticing / had noticed) that Gajaraj looked happy the very first morning after the dog arrived.
3. Write your own sentence: Neither _____________ nor _____________ _____________ (add a verb) when Buntee finally raced back to the stable.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. was missing — the past progressive shows the ongoing state of longing at the moment the farmer arrived. 2. noticed — simple past for a completed observation at a specific moment. 3. Accepted answers use 'neither … nor' correctly with two noun phrases and a verb; for example, 'Neither the mahout nor the farmer could believe how fast Buntee ran.'

items.item_stem:
The news report discussed in class tells of Tarra the elephant and Bella the dog at an elephant sanctuary in the United States. When Bella was injured and kept inside a building for three weeks, Tarra stood outside and waited for her. Write a response to the following questions in three to four sentences:

What does Tarra's behaviour during those three weeks tell us about animal friendship? How is this similar to what Gajaraj does in the story when Buntee is taken away?

expected_elements: Identifies Tarra's waiting as evidence of loyalty and emotional bond.
Connects Tarra's behaviour to Gajaraj refusing food after separation.
Draws an explicit similarity between the two animal friendships.
Writes in complete sentences with a clear, reasoned response.

items.source_context: Jataka tale origins; elephants in Indian culture; Tarra-and-Bella real-life elephant-dog friendship.
items.item_stem:
The story of Gajaraj and Buntee is adapted from a Jataka tale — ancient Buddhist wisdom stories retold for over two thousand years. The class also discussed how elephants have played important roles in Indian culture, festivals, and history, and how their lives are affected by human activity today.

Prepare a short project on ONE of the following:
(a) Find another Jataka story. Write a brief summary and explain what life value or lesson it teaches.
(b) Create a fact-file about elephants in India: include two cultural or historical roles they have played and two challenges they face today because of human activity.

Present your findings to the class in four to five sentences or a labelled fact-file card.

expected_elements: Option (a): names a specific Jataka story with a clear summary.
Option (a): states the lesson or value the story teaches explicitly.
Option (b): gives two distinct cultural or historical roles of elephants.
Option (b): identifies two real ecological or human-conflict challenges elephants face.
